parties.name: Freedom Party of Austria
parties.description:
Right-wing populist party, formed in 1955-1956 as successor of [[atVdU|Federation of Independents]], representing pan-Germanists and national liberals opposed to socialism and Catholic clericalism, represented by the [[atSPO|Social Democratic Party of Austria]] (SPÖ) and the [[atOVP|Austrian People's Party]] (ÖVP), respectively. Its first leader, Anton Reinthaller, was a former Nazi functionary and SS officer, but the FPÖ did not advocate far-right policies and presented itself as a centrist party. The FPÖ was long the third largest in Austria and had modest support. Under the leadership of Norbert Steger in the early 1980s, it sought to style itself on Germany's [[deFDP|Free Democratic Party]] (FDP) The FPÖ gave external support to SPÖ chancellor Bruno Kreisky (SPÖ) after the 1970 election and joined Fred Sinowatz's government, as the SPÖ's junior partner, after the 1983 election.
 
 Jörg Haider became leader of the party in 1986, after which it began an ideological turn towards right-wing populism. This resulted in a strong surge in electoral support, but also led the SPÖ to break ties, and a splinter in the form of the [[atLiF|Liberal Forum]] in 1993. In the 1999 election, the FPÖ won 26.9% of the vote, becoming the second-most popular party, ahead of the ÖVP by around 500 votes. The two parties eventually reached a coalition agreement in which the ÖVP retained the office of chancellor. The FPÖ soon lost most of its popularity, falling to 10% in the 2002 election, but remained in government as junior partner. Internal tensions led Haider and much of the party leadership to leave in 2005, forming the [[atBZO|Alliance for the Future of Austria]] (BZÖ), which replaced the FPÖ as governing partner. Heinz-Christian Strache then became leader, and the party gradually regained its popularity, peaking at 26.0% in the 2017 election. The FPÖ once again became junior partner in government with the ÖVP. In May 2019, the Ibiza affair led to the collapse of the government and the resignation of Strache from both the offices of vice-chancellor and party leader. The resulting snap election saw the FPÖ fall to 16.2% and return to opposition. On 30 June 2024, ANO 2011, the Freedom Party of Austria, and [[huFidesz|Fidesz]] created a new alliance named [[euPfE|Patriots for Europe]].

parties.name: People's Union
parties.description:
Big tent flemish nationalist party, preceded by the electoral alliance [[beCVV|Christian Flemish People's Union]] (CVV).

On 13 October 2001 the party openly split into three factions: the progressive wing around Bert Anciaux, the conservative nationalist wing around Geert Bourgeois, and a centrist group opposing the imminent split. An internal referendum was held on the future of the party.

The right wing won a large plurality at a party referendum, with 47 percent. However, while it inherited VU's structure, it did not take the VU name due to falling short of a majority and not being allowed to use the party name under Belgian electoral law. Instead, it reconstituted itself as a new party, and re-registered itself as the [[beNVA|New Flemish Alliance]] (N-VA). 

The left wing under Anciaux broke off and became [[beSLP|Spirit]], while the liberal members joined the [[beAnders|Flemish Liberals and Democrats]] (VLD). The two parties proceeded to form new electoral alliances, known in Belgium as cartels, with the N-VA allying with [[be        CD&V|Christian Democratic and Flemish]] and Spirit with the [[beVooruit|Socialist Party – Different]] (sp.a). These cartels broke up in 2008 as the parties continued their decline, until the N-VA experienced a sudden resurgence in 2009, eventually becoming the largest party in Flanders and going on to participate as a coalition partner in the Belgian government, while Spirit ceased to exist, merging with [[beGroen|Groen]].

parties.name: Vlaams Blok
parties.description:
The party originated from split within the [[beVU|Volksunie]] (VU) party after the right-wing separatist and national conservative wing became disgruntled with the compromise of accepting Belgian federalism over Flemish interests, and what they saw as the VU's move to the left. 

The former VU members created the [[beVNP|Flemish National Party]] (VNP) and the [[beVVP|Flemish People's Party]] (VVP) which formed an electoral alliance called Vlaams Blok in 1978, before merging to create Vlaams Blok as a political party in 1979. 

Vlaams Blok was the most notable militant right wing of the Flemish movement and its track record in the Flemish and Belgian parliament elections was strong, making it one of the most successful nationalist parties in Western Europe and it ultimately surpassed the People's Union in support. 

The party initially focused solely on the issues of Flemish autonomy and political freedom, which remained its core philosophy, but subsequently gained wider public support through broadening its campaigns to include immigration and law-and-order themes.

Following a 1989 agreement, known as the cordon sanitaire, the party was effectively blocked from entering any level of government. 

The court of appeal in Ghent in April 2004 ruled that some of the party's organizations had breached the 1981 anti-racism law and that the party sanctioned discrimination. The ruling was made definite on 9 November 2004, and the party shortly after reorganised itself as the [[beVB|Vlaams Belang]]. By 2004, the party had arguably become the single most popular Flemish party in Belgium, supported by about one in four of the Flemish electorate, as well as being one of the most successful radical right-wing populist parties in Europe as a whole.

parties.name: Defenders of the Homeland
parties.description:
During the first half of 2025, groups supporting Abelardo de la Espriella's presidential candidacy organized on social media and at regional events as part of the campaign. On 16 July 2025, De la Espriella registered the "Defenders of the Homeland" campaign committee with the National Registry, with the goal of collecting signatures for an independent presidential candidacy. The chosen slogan was "Firm for the Homeland."

On 31 May 2026, the movement came in first place in the presidential elections with a total of 10,361,499 votes, representing 43.74% of the total valid votes, which allowed them to advance to the second round and compete against Iván Cepeda. In that instance, Abelardo de la Espriella was the candidate with the most votes, becoming the president-elect of Colombia, a position he will assume on 7 August 2026.

On 3 August 2026, with 6 votes in favor, 1 against, and 2 abstentions, the plenary session of the National Electoral Council approved the organization's legal status. Thus, it officially became a political party.

parties.name: Our Czechia
parties.description:
A centre-right political party in the Czech Republic, founded by South Bohemian Governor Martin Kuba.

Kuba left the [[czODS|Civic Democratic Party]] (ODS) in November 2025 after 22 years as a member. He announced his intention to form a new party, declaring that ODS could not be "fixed" anymore. Senators Zbyněk Sýkora, and Tomáš Fiala, České Budějovice Mayor Dagmar Škodová Parmová, and former South Bohemian governor Jan Zahradník also suspended their ODS membership and followed Kuba to the new movement. 30 of the 34 South Bohemian representatives elected on the ODS candidate list in the regional elections in September 2024 also expressed their intention to join the new movement. There has also been speculation that Pardubice Governor Martin Netolický, former Moravian-Silesian governor Ivo Vondrák, and former Pilsen Governor Rudolf Špoták are also ready to cooperate with the movement.

Kuba registered 'Our Czechia' as a trademark, and formally announced his party on 2 February 2026. Journalists pointed out that the name 'Our Czechia' had been used by one of the funds of the J&T Group for several years.

On 13 April 2026, Kuba announced on Facebook that the party would cooperate with Netolický's party Us in the 2026 Czech municipal elections, and intended to cooperate in the next parliamentary election. Netolický announced that the parties would also cooperate in the 2026 Czech Senate election.

parties.name: Amanat
parties.description:
The ruling [[kzNurOtan|Nur Otan]] party of Kazakstan was renamed to Amanat on 1 March 2022, following former President Nursultan Nazarbayev's retirement from active politics and the bloody January protests.

After Nazarbayev's withdrawal from active politics in 2022, Mäjilis chairman Erlan Qoşanov assumed the position of party leadership, becoming the first non-executive official to chair Amanat, following a brief tenure by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. 

Despite this leadership transition, Amanat remained a party of power, continuing to align towards Tokayev's administration. The party strongly supported Tokayev's constitutional reforms in the 2022 referendum that aimed at shifting to a more balanced president-parliamentary system, while also backing his successful independent campaign bid during the 2022 snap presidential election as part of the [[kzPC|People's Coalition]]. 

From 2023, Amanat had maintained its majority control of the Mäjilis, playing a central role in the nation's political and economic developments.[21] In June 2026, Amanat voted to dissolve its independent structure at an extraordinary congress, choosing to merge into the newly established Ädilet party ahead of the 2026 legislative election.[22]

During its existence, Amanat had been described as a big tent party, generally leaning conservative, with a focus on stability, national unity, and economic development. It promoted reforms in areas such as civil service, economic diversification, and the rule of law. The party's governance style had been described as authoritarian, with critics noting restrictions on political freedoms and limited opposition.

Amanat had a widespread presence across Kazakhstan's administrative divisions and held numerous local offices, maintaining legislative control through deputy groups in local assemblies (mäslihats) throughout the country.

On 14 June 2026 Amanat merged into newly-formed [[kzAdilet|Ädilet]] party.

parties.description:
A liberal-conservative political party in Kazakhstan. 

Aq Jol was formed in early 2002, after its faction became being split from the [[kzQDT|Democratic Choice of Kazakhstan]]. From there, it was positioned as an opposition party though in a moderate tone. The party has experienced fragmentation over the years, leading to the formation of dissident factions. Despite its opposition stance, the Aq Jol had been repeatedly described as a pro-government party in Kazakhstan, with it joining the [[kzPC|People's Coalition]] in support of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in the 2022 election. The party has been led by Azat Peruaşev for many years.

The Aq Jol party advocates for political reform, economic liberalism, and secularism. It has participated in presidential and parliamentary elections, with varying levels of electoral success.

The party also advocates to lead the way for Kazakhstan to join the European Union in the future.[3]

parties.name: Auyl
parties.description:
It was originally founded by Gani Qaliev on 30 January 2000 before eventually merging with the [[kzQPP|Party of Patriots of Kazakhstan]] on 5 September 2015. Auyl has participated in every Kazakh parliamentary election since 2004 and nominated presidential candidate Toleutai Raqymbekov in the 2019 presidential election. 

It first entered the Mäjilis at the 2023 legislative election, winning eight seats and becoming the largest opposition party.

The Auyl declared its main values of spirituality, patriotism, loyalty, equality, cooperation. Basing its principles of social democracy, the party spoke out in favour of the rural population's interests by seeing its priorities as strengthening state regulation and supporting the agricultural economy, protecting the interests of rural workers, actively promoting the implementation of economic and political reforms aimed at further democratization of society, the implementation of justified forms of market relations in all sectors of the economy, improving the living standards of citizens, as well as the formation of patriotic education of the population.[2] It is supportive of incumbent President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev,[3] and has been accused of being controlled opposition and a front for agribusiness.

The party outlined its goal to promote the construction of an independent strong and prosperous Kazakhstan, with a high standard of living for all Kazakhstanis, in order to embark on the path of globalization, preserve the national spirit, cultural and spiritual potential and traditions, language and religion, as well as be open to new technologies.

parties.description:
The party emerged due to a split in the [[kzQKP|Communist Party of Kazakhstan]] (QKP). The idea to create a new party belongs to the 12 members of the Central Committee of Communist Party of Kazakhstan, who withdrew its membership because of the disagreements with the First Secretary of the QKP's Central Committee Serikbolsyn Abdildin. The reason for the split with the QKP was the election of a Secretary and a member of Mazhilis Tolen Tokhtassynov. About 15,000 members left QKP for QKHP. The founding congress QKHP took place in April 2004, on 21 June 2004 the party was registered with the Ministry of Justice of Kazakhstan.

Following the elections to Mazhilis in 2004, the party received 1.98% of total voters (proportional system) and did not pass into Parliament.

In the 2005 presidential elections, QKHP nominated Erasyl Abilqasymov as its candidate who received 0.34% of the votes.

On 28 March 2007 the QKHP and the QPK held a joint press conference at which they announced an impending merger. QKHP subsequently abandoned the association with the QPK because of the sharp political differences.[4] At a press conference in June 2007, the First Secretary of QKHP Vladislav Kosarev named the fact that the Communist Party of Kazakhstan was considering associations with QKHP only at the highest level (Bureaus of Central Committee) as the main reason for refusing to merge, at the same time according to him consideration for such merger was not provided at local level. Kosarev said also that structures of QKP had been completely destroyed and the authority of the party among the people has been reduced to zero-level.

In elections to Mazhilis in 2007, the party won 1.29% of total votes and did not pass the electoral threshold to Parliament. In the 2012 election, the party won 7.19% of vote and 7 seats to become one of three parties to enter Parliament. Despite being officially in opposition, the party is considered as loyal to the regime and often votes with the government.

The 15th Communist People's Party of Kazakhstan Extraordinary Congress was held on 11 November 2020 in the capital Nur-Sultan. Delegates to the congress voted to rename the party the [[kzQHP|People's Party of Kazakhstan]] (QHP). Several changes were also made to the charters and programs of the party. The party also elected new leadership and began to declare itself social democratic.

parties.description:
At the 15th Extraordinary Congress of the [[kzQKHP|Communist People's Party of Kazakhstan]] held on 11 November 2020, a decision was made to rename the QKHP to the People's Party of Kazakhstan, with corresponding amendments to the party's charter and program. This decision was motivated by a desire to expand the party's electoral support ahead of the 2021 Kazakh legislative election. The Extraordinary Congress held a quorum of 33 delegates from the party. Every delegate voted in favour of the name change except Honorary Secretary Vladislav Kosarev. The party's parliamentary leader Aiqyn Qongyrov was unanimously chosen to be Chairman of the QHP, succeeding Kosarev who served as the QKHP's de facto leader since June 2013, while Jambyl Ahmetbekov, Turgyn Syzdyqov, Viktor Smirnov, and Gauhar Nugmanova were chosen to be Secretaries of the QHP.

Officially, the People's Party of Kazakhstan positions itself as a center-left political force, proclaiming the principles of social democracy and renewed socialism. Its program declares its commitment to the ideas of social justice, equality, social solidarity, and strengthening the role of the state in the economy and social spheres.

On 28 March 2022, at the XIX extraordinary congress of the party, Ermūhamet Ertısbaev was elected as the Chairman of the People's Party of Kazakhstan.

In October 2022, the QHP joined the [[kzPC|People's Coalition]], in support of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, ceasing to be even nominally part of the opposition.

On an Almaty press conference of 1 July 2024,[ some members of the party demanded the resignation of Ermukhamet Ertisbaev from party chairmanship. The party infighting is said to come from the apparently "emerging personality cult" of Ertisbaev. Former deputy chairman, Ashat Asylbekov also claimed, that on one of the interviews that neared the 2023 Kazakh local elections, Ertisbaev stated that he'd be forever loyal to Nursultan Nazarbayev. These acts of Ertisbaev are said to be damaging to the party's reputation and Asylbekov, Almaty branch chairman Töleujan Jündibaev and Mangystau Region representative Abdraşit Niyaz publicly criticised the chairman and his deputy Miras Aukenov and demanded an "extraordinary" congress. Ertisbaev's large spendings on his "Ertisbaev live" YouTube channel and his public support for Quandyq Bishimbaev during his trial had also greatly damaged the party's reputation, Asylbekov says.

On 7 June 2026, at an extraordinary congress of the People's Party of Kazakhstan, a new chairman, Nursultan Şoqanov, was elected, and the party's charter and new identity were approved. During the congress, former QHP chairman Ermukhamet Ertisbaev noted that the party's official digital platforms currently unite more than 1.1 million subscribers, the total reach of publications exceeds 600 million views, and the number of comments and requests has reached approximately 1 million, with these figures continuing to grow.

Ahora Nación was founded on 13 May 2023, under the leadership of Alfonso López-Chau, former rector of the National University of Engineering (UNI), who became known for sheltering protesters at the university where he served as rector.

Two Ahora Nación congresspeople of 2021-2026 Congress were part of the [[peBDP|People's Democratic Bloc]] parliamentary group.

AN managed to win four seats in the Senate and ten in the Chamber of Deputies during the 2026 election. In a presidential race, López-Chau finished seventh with 7.29% of voted.

parties.description:
Belmont was his OBRAS party's candidate in the 1995 presidential election, but received only 2% of the vote. In the Congress of the Republic, OBRAS won two seats out of 120.

In the 2006 general election, Belmont was an independent candidate on the [[peFC|Centre Front]] list of Valentín Paniagua, but failed to secure a seat. However, in 2009, he entered Congress as a replacement following the death of congressman Alberto Andrade, the former mayor of Lima.

In 2015, OBRAS formed an alliance with the [[peSU|Siempre Unidos]] party, and in 2016 with [[pePPS|Peru Secure Homeland]], with the aim of participating in the 2016 presidential election; however, this alliance ended with the withdrawal of candidate Renzo Reggiardo.

In the 2018 Lima municipal election, OBRAS ran within the [[pePL|Libertarian Peru]] party, with Belmont as the mayoral candidate, receiving 3.89% of the vote.

In 2020, Belmont and his movement joined the ethnocacerist [[peUPP|Union for Peru]], becoming the number one candidate on the Lima UPP list in the snap congressional election.

That same year, with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, Belmont began organizing COVID-19 denialist marches and promoting anti-vaccination slogans such as "Every vaccine you take [...] could make you infertile."

In 2021, Belmont again allied with [[pePL|Free Peru]], becoming an adviser to President Pedro Castillo. Despite the fact that a week before his appointment, Belmont described Castillo as "another one of those who ends up in jail or gets rich and flees the country."

In July 2024, the party was re-registered with the National Jury of Elections to participate in the next general election.

Belmont, the party leader, has become OBRAS's presidential candidate for the 2026 election. In his campaign, Belmont typically wears a Spartan warrior helmet, and his supporters refer to themselves as "Spartans".

During Belmont's OBRAS campaign, the party adopted some ideas from the government of Andrés Manuel López Obrador, former President of Mexico, such as the "Abrazos, no balazos" policy and the implementation of a government conference system similar to "Las Mañaneras del Pueblo" as its main proposals.

parties.name: Party of Good Government
parties.description:
The party was founded on 29 January 2020, by sociologist Jorge Nieto, former minister of Defense and of Culture under the presidency of Pedro Pablo Kuczynski. The party's name and Inti (Inca sun god) symbolism both alude to the 17th century illustrated chronicle El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno, authored by Quechua nobleman Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala. Nieto has described the chronicle as remarkably relevant to contemporary Peru, particularly for its denunciation of the enduring divide between the Indigenous and criollo worlds and its call for cultural equality and equal rights.

On 10 July 2024, Nieto announced the party's registration with the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) of the National Elections Board (JNE) with the aim of participating in the 2026 general election. It achieved its registration on 2 August 2024, becoming the 33rd political party registered with the ROP.

In the 2026 general election, the PBG came in fourth place in its presidential candidacy and won seats in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, securing the fourth and third largest blocs in each chamber, respectively. The party, under the leadership of Jorge Nieto, decided not to endorse either of the two candidates in the presidential runoff between the leftist Roberto Sánchez of [[peJP|Together for Peru]] and the rightist Keiko Fujimori of the [[peFP|Popular Force]], and, on the contrary, actively promoted spoiled ballots, urging its supporters to write "We want a Good Government" on the ballots. Nieto also questioned the "lesser evil" argument for choosing between the two candidates as problematic and maintained that "the left has to take responsibility for the consequences of permanently choosing the lesser evil."

The party was founded on 29 January 2020, by sociologist Jorge Nieto, former minister of Defense and of Culture under the presidency of Pedro Pablo Kuczynski. The party's name and Inti (Inca sun god) symbolism both alude to the 17th century illustrated chronicle El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno, authored by Quechua nobleman Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala. Nieto has described the chronicle as remarkably relevant to contemporary Peru, particularly for its denunciation of the enduring divide between the Indigenous and criollo worlds and its call for cultural equality and equal rights.

On 10 July 2024, Nieto announced the party's registration with the Registry of Political Organizations (ROP) of the National Elections Board (JNE) with the aim of participating in the 2026 general election. It achieved its registration on 2 August 2024, becoming the 33rd political party registered with the ROP.

In the 2026 general election, the PBG came in fourth place in its presidential candidacy and won seats in the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies, securing the fourth and third largest blocs in each chamber, respectively. The party, under the leadership of Jorge Nieto, decided not to endorse either of the two candidates in the presidential runoff between the leftist Roberto Sánchez of [[peJP|Together for Peru]] and the rightist Keiko Fujimori of the [[peFP|Popular Force]], and, on the contrary, actively promoted spoiled ballots, urging its supporters to write "We want a Good Government" on the ballots. Nieto also questioned the "lesser evil" argument for choosing between the two candidates as problematic and maintained that "the left has to take responsibility for the consequences of permanently choosing the lesser evil."

parties.name: Together for Peru
parties.description:
Political party and political coalition.

In May 2017, the organizations of the [[peUnete|Únete]] front ([[peFS|Social Force]], [[peCxC|Citizens for Change]], [[pePCP-PR|Communist Party of Peru – Red Fatherland]], [[pePCP|Peruvian Communist Party – Unity]], and [[peMS|Movement for Socialism]])[4] and the [[pePHP|Peruvian Humanist Party]] (PHP) decided to form a political party under the latter's electoral registration. It would henceforth be known as Juntos por el Perú (Together for Peru). Roberto Sánchez ([[pePHP|PHP]]) was registered as president and Gonzalo García Núñez ([[peFS|Social Force]]) as general secretary.

Looking ahead to the 2018 regional and municipal elections, Together for Peru formed an alliance with the [[peNP|New Peru]] movement. It won 10 district mayoralties. This alliance remained in place for the 2020-2021 supplementary congressional elections, but failed to win any seats.

For the 2021 general elections, JP unsuccessfully nominated Verónika Mendoza, leader of [[peNP|New Peru]], for president. The alliance won five seats: four for [[peNP|New Peru]] and one for Together for Peru (Roberto Sánchez). Before, during, and after the election, JP faced internal divisions. [[peFC|Citizen Force]] (a union between [[peFS|Social Force]] and [[peCxC|CxC]]) decided to join the [[pePM|Purple Party]]. The [[pePHP|PHP]]) opted to support Pedro Castillo's candidacy ([[pePL|PL]]) in the first round and officially withdrew from JP in December 2021.[[pePCP-PR|PCP – Red Fatherland]] followed suit around the same time. Members of [[peNP|New Peru]] resigned from JP starting in September 2021. [[pePCP|PCP – Unity]] withdrew from the coalition the following year.

In the Congress of the Republic, the parliamentary group Together for Peru has undergone several changes in its composition. Initially, it was known as [[peBDP|Democratic Change–Together for Peru]], which included Roberto Sánchez of JP and the four congressmen from [[peNP|New Peru]]. This group was later joined by dissidents from [[pePL|Free Peru]]: Guillermo Bermejo, Hamlet Echevarría, Roberto Kamiche, and Nieves Limachi. Congresswoman Susel Paredes also joined later. Following the withdrawal of the [[pePL|Free Peru]] congressmen, including Paredes, from the caucus, congressmen from the teachers' union, linked to Pedro Castillo, joined. With this, the parliamentary group became known as Together for Peru – [[peVP|Voices of the People]] - [[peBMCN|Magisterial Bloc]].

From 2022 onward, Together for Peru would be composed solely of a dissident faction of the [[pePHP|PHP]] under the leadership of Roberto Sánchez. In the subnational elections of that year, it won four provincial mayoralties for the first time (Santa in Áncash, Calca and La Convención in Cusco, and Chiclayo in Lambayeque) and 38 district mayoralties.

For the 2026 general elections, Together for Peru registered the candidacy of its leader, Roberto Sánchez, for the presidency of Peru. They would do so in alliance with [[peTCP|Todo con el Pueblo]] (Everything with the People) of former president Pedro Castillo and the [[peANTAURO|National Alliance]] of ethnocacerist Antauro Humala. The coalition was named Together with the People (Juntos con el Pueblo, also abbreviated JP). [[peVP|Voices of the People]], JP's allies in Congress, ran in a coalition with [[peNP|New Peru]], JP's former allies, under the name [[peVenceremos|Venceremos]].

On the parliamentary lists, Together for Peru included Pedro Castillo's adopted daughter, Yenifer Paredes, and his siblings, José Mercedes Castillo and Inés Castillo. Former members of Castillo's government (Íber Maraví, Anahí Durand, Hernando Cevallos, and Walter Ayala) and congressmen who supported the former president (Víctor Cutipa, Pasión Dávila, Margot Palacios, Jaime Quito, Silvana Robles, and Elías Varas) also ran. Antauro Humala's father, Isaac Humala, and ethnocacerist allies such as "Pepe" Feria and Marlon Aguirre were also candidates for JP.

Due to irregularities in the receipt of contributions, the National Elections Board fined Juntos por el Perú S/ 175,000 and reduced its electoral airtime allocation.

Sanchez advanced to the second round, and Together for Peru placed second in seats in both houses of Congress. In June 2026, Sanchez was defeated by Keiko Fujimori of [[peFP|Popular Force]].

parties.name: Civic Initiative
parties.description:
The founder and leader of the party, Andrey Nechayev, was the Minister of Economic Development from 1991 to 1994.

In 2018 presidential election, GRANI nominated Ksenia Sobchak. She finished 4th with 1.68% of vote.

On 13 March 2018, Vedomosti reported that Ksenia Sobchak and Dmitry Gudkov would announce the creation of a new right-wing party based on the Civil Initiative on March 15. Since then, the party has encountered legal problems with the Ministry of Justice, resulting in an informal rebranding.

On 23 June 2018, the Third (reorganizational) Congress took place, where a decision was made to create a new "Party of Changes" based on the Civil Initiative. Ksenia Sobchak and Dmitry Gudkov were appointed to the party's top positions.

On 1 March 2019, the youth movement "St. Petersburg – City of Changes!" was created in St. Petersburg with the aim of countering the Party of Changes's activities in the city during the municipal and gubernatorial elections. The Ministry of Justice refused to recognize the party's reorganization and deliberately obstructed its reorganization. In April 2019, it became known that Sobchak had ceased funding the Party of Changes. In March 2020, Dmitry Gudkov left the party, not wanting to interfere with the struggle to preserve the structure. Nechayev became the party's chairman again, and the name was restored to its previous form.

Boris Nadezhdin is a former member of the Russia State Duma and currently Moscow Oblast's local politician. On 6 October 2023, Nadezhdin's participation in the election was announced by Dmitry Kisiev, founder of the Candidates’ Headquarters, on his social media. On 31 October 2023, Nadezhdin publicly announced that he will run from the Civic Initiative party. He was not admitted to the election.

On 17 June 2025, the Supreme Court of Russia liquidated the party. Representatives of the Civil Initiative attempted to appeal this decision. Following the appeal, the Supreme Court upheld the decision on 30 September 2025.

On 19 October, the deregistered Civil Initiative announced the creation of its own youth organization.

In December 2025, Nechayev announced his intention to re-register the party. On 18 December, the Civil Initiative announced the registration of its organizing committee with the Russian Ministry of Justice.

parties.name: Civic Platform
parties.description:
Civic Platform was founded on 4 June 2012, by former members of the [[ruPD|Right Cause]] (PD) party who broke away from PD after it was seized by forces affiliated with the Presidential Administration. The party was initially led by businessman and oligarch Mikhail Prokhorov, who ran as an independent candidate in the 2011 presidential election, finishing third.

Initially, the party positioned itself as a pan-democratic, non-ideological umbrella party, or described as liberal. However, by 2015, it was "softly captured" by pro-government forces, leading to the departure of several members, including its founder, and the party itself becoming right-wing conservative and Putinist.

The party participated in the State Duma elections in 2016 and 2021. In both cases, the party's list garnered less than 1% of the vote, failing to cross the 5% electoral threshold. Rifat Shaikhutdinov was elected MP twice in a single-mandate constituency. Since October 2021, Shaikhutdinov has been a member of the [[ruLDPR|LDPR]] faction.

On 30 April 2026, the Supreme Court of Russia suspended the party's activities for three months after upholding a claim by the Russian Ministry of Justice. As a result, the party was barred from running in the 2026 State Duma election.

parties.name: Civilian Power
parties.description:
The party was founded by Alexander Ryavkin, president of the Russian medical corporation DENAS MS.

From 2002 to 2004, it was called the "Russian Network Party of Small and Medium Businesses."

From April 2004 to 2007, it was known as the "Free Russia" party.

In the elections of December 4, 2005, the party participated in the elections to the Moscow City Duma, gaining 2.22% (not gaining the required 10%). In its election campaign, it focused on anti-campaigning against the [[ruYabloko|Yabloko]] party with videos like “Don’t vote for Yabloko, it’s rotten!”

On October 8, 2006, the party overtook the 7% barrier on the legislative elections in Novgorod District. In November 2006, the 6th party conference was held. On February 27, 2007, Mikhail Barshchevsky, the chairman and plenipotentiary of the High Council of the Russian government, held a press conference. This was in aid of the party principles of Civilian Power. In the middle of April 2007, an organizational conference was held.

The chairman of the High Council is plenipotentiary of the Government of Russia in Constitutional, Supreme and Highest Arbitral Courts Mikhail Barshchevsky (a member since December 2006). The chairman of the Federal Political Council − The founder of the party, businessman Alexander Ryavkin from 2014 - 2015 year was the vice governor of Oryol Oblast.

The party won 1.05% of votes in the 2007 elections, not breaking the 7% barrier, and thus no seats in duma.

Civilian Power supported Dmitry Medvedev as their candidate in the presidential election in 2008.

It merged with [[ruSPS|Union of Right Forces]] and the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] to form the [[ruPD|Right Cause]] on 16 November 2008.

Civilian Power was again registered as a political party on 7 June 2012. After its dissolution, it was transformed into the All-Russian public organization "Civilian Forces", which collaborated with one of the projects of the [[ruREPZ|Russian Ecological Party "The Greens"]], the organization "Green Patrol".

In the elections of 2014, the party won one seat in the regional parliament of Nenets Autonomous Okrug.

On 13 December 2015, Civilian Power Party Chairman Oleg Sidorov and [[ruRPSS|Communist Party of Social Justice]] Chairman Andrei Bogdanov announced at a joint meeting of the parties' Federal Political Councils their upcoming merger under the existing name "Communist Party of Social Justice," but using the organizational base of the Civil Power Party, which had been admitted to 2016 federal elections without collecting signatures. However, on 18 December 2015, Oleg Sidorov was removed from office.

In 2018, she did not nominate her own candidate in the presidential elections, supporting the current President Vladimir Putin.

In the 2019 Chelyabinsk Oblast gubernatorial elections, Alexey Sevastyanov became the party's candidate, which caused a scandal, some party representatives claimed that Civilian Power had not nominated him. However, he was still registered and received 3.23% of the vote in the elections.

At the end of November 2024, the Ministry of Justice of Russia appealed to the Supreme Court, demanding the liquidation of the Civilian Power political party. The Ministry of Justice argued that the party had not nominated candidates for federal elections for a long time and had hardly participated in local elections. On 15 January 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the appeal, dissolving the party.

description.text:

From 2002 to 2004, it was called the "Russian Network Party of Small and Medium Businesses."

From April 2004 to 2007, it was known as the "Free Russia" party.

parties.description:
Republican branch of the [[suCPSU|Communist Party of the Soviet Union]] in the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. Established on 19 June 1990 (before that, the RSFSR remained the only republic of the Soviet Union that did not have a republican communist party). The CP RSFSR was not an independent party and did not have its own charter or program.

Politically, CP RSFSR became a centre for communist opponents of Gorbachev's CPSU leadership.

The August putsch (19-21 August 1991) served as the basis for accusing the CPSU of unconstitutional activity. By decree of RSFSR President Boris Yeltsin on 6 November 1991, the activities of the CPSU and its republican organization, the CP RSFSR, were terminated, and their property was confiscated. However, the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation issued a ruling on 30 November 1992, declaring the ban on the activities of the primary organizations of the CPSU/CP RSFSR unconstitutional.

Despite the ban, the party's activities continued until February 1993, when a restoration congress was held. Based on the primary organizations, the CPSU RSFSR was re-established as the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]].

parties.description:
Communists of Russia was founded on 23 May 2009, as a public association. Its founders were the Independent Union of Communist Youth of the Russian Federation (NSKM RF), the Communists of Saint Petersburg and the Leningrad Oblast (KPLO), and the Communists of the Far East (KDV).

On 22 May 2011, the Second Congress of the Communists of Russia organization was held. Representatives of the [[ruRKRPKPSS|RKRP–RPK]] attended the congress. A decision was made to begin transforming the organization into a political party. Maxim Suraikin was elected First Secretary of the Central Committee. Some party organs of the [[ruVKPB|All-Russian Communist Party of the Future]] were transferred to the party.

On 22 April 2012, the Third Congress of the organization was held, at which a decision was made to transform the organization into a political party. The party was registered by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation on 14 June 2012.

The party's main rival on the left is the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] (KPRF). KPKR considers itself an alternative to the KPRF, which it believes is no longer a Marxist party and will not be able to return to power as long as Gennady Zyuganov is First Secretary. However, the KPKR party has been widely described as a spoiler party, including by the KPRF.

In May 2016, the party held the founding congress of the public organization "Atheists of Russia." According to Suraykin, Russian atheists "are practically not represented in the public sphere".

Since the summer of 2018, the party has actively participated in protests against pension reform, both in the capital and in the regions.

Following the 9 September 2018, elections, the party overcame the 5% threshold in the elections for deputies to regional parliaments in five constituent entities of the Russian Federation: the Republic of Khakassia: 8.01% (2 out of 50 seats), the Nenets Autonomous Okrug: 5.29% (1 out of 19 seats), the Rostov Region: 5.06% (1 out of 60 seats), the Ulyanovsk Region: 5.83% (1 out of 36 seats), and the Yaroslavl Region: 6.63% (1 out of 50 seats). It also gained seats in many local government bodies, including the Abakan Council of Deputies, the Council of People's Deputies of the Maykop Urban District, and others.

On 8 September 2019, the Communists of Russia party received 5.67% of the vote in the Tula Regional Duma elections (1 seat out of 36).

On 13 September 2020, the Communists of Russia party received 7.47% of the vote in the Rostov-on-Don City Duma elections.

Following the September 19, 2021, elections, the party cleared the 5% threshold in the regional parliamentary elections in three constituent entities of the Russian Federation: Altai Krai with 12.1% (4 seats out of 68), Amur Oblast with 8.3% (1 seat out of 27), and Omsk Oblast with 11% (3 seats out of 44).

In the 2021 State Duma elections, the party placed 8th, receiving 1.27% of the vote.

On 18 March 2022, an extraordinary party congress was held, at which Sergei Malinkovich, the new chairman of the KPKR Central Committee, was elected. The change in party leadership was confirmed by the Ministry of Justice, although Suraykin did not recognize this congress. On 28 December 2023, Malinkovich was nominated by an overwhelming majority as the party candidate for president of Russia in the 2024 presidential election. Malinkovich promised a program like Stalin's ten blows, against United States capitalism and imperialism, and for victory in Russia's war against Ukraine.

Казачья партия Российской Федерации
Kazach'ya partiya Rossiyskoy Federatsii
parties.description:
In October 2012, the head of the Council for Cossack Affairs, Alexander Beglov (future Mayor of Saint Petersburg), announced the creation of the Cossack Party of the Russian Federation. The idea of ​​a Cossack party provoked a negative reaction among politicians, the public, and the Cossacks themselves. The [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] (KPRF), for example, drew attention to the fact that its initials completely coincided with those of the new organization. This raised suspicions of creating a so-called "spoiler." The KPRF even attempted to rename KaPRF through the courts, but to no avail.

The first Supreme Ataman of the Union of Cossacks of Russia, Alexander Martynov, believes that the creation of the party is not a Cossack initiative, but a local one.

The founding congress of the Cossack Party of the Russian Federation was held on 24 November 2012. 96 delegates voted in favor of the party's creation, with only one voting against. Rostov Region Vice-Governor Sergei Bondarev, a former member of [[ruER|United Russia]], was elected chairman of the new party. The congress concluded with an Orthodox Christian prayer service.

In 2015, Bondarev was replaced as chairman of the KaPRF by Nikolai Konstantinov, a longtime friend of Alexander Beglov.

In 2015, the Leningrad Regional Branch of the KaPRF announced its intention to nominate a candidate for the gubernatorial election in the Leningrad Oblast. He turned out to be Vitaly Martynenko, then a member of the St. Petersburg Legislative Assembly and now deputy head of the Vasileostrovsky District Administration. However, the matter never progressed beyond talk. Martynenko was not a member of the CPRF and was a member of [[ruER|United Russia]].

In 2016, the Leningrad Oblast Electoral Commission certified the lists of candidates for the local Legislative Assembly of the 6th convocation. Among the candidates registered was the regional branch of the CPRF. This was a significant breakthrough for the party, and its representatives could appear in the regional parliament for the first time. The regional list was headed by Andrei Sorokvashin, then an independent deputy in the Semenovsky MO in the Admiralty District of St. Petersburg.

The KaPRF continues to periodically participate in elections across Russia, but cannot boast of any significant successes. The party can be used to promote people loyal to Beglov into parliamentary positions, facilitated by the fact that it is headed by the governor's personal friend, Nikolai Konstantinov. However, the party does not play a significant role in the political life of St. Petersburg, although it has attempted to promote city politicians to the leadership of the neighboring Leningrad Region.

parties.nativeName:
Демократическая партия России
Demokraticheskaya partiya Rossii
parties.description:
The Democratic Party of Russia was founded by Nikolay Travkin. Other early leaders included Stanislav Govorukhin and Sergey Glazyev. In the 1990s it was a prominent democratically oriented party holding seats in the first State Duma and was a member of the [[ruDR|Democratic Russia]] coalition. After the coup in 1991, the party evolved from liberal anticommunism to centrism (1992–1993) and later to moderate Russian nationalism (1994–1995).

In 1991, the Democratic Party differed from other liberal/democratic organizations with its 'demopatriotic' stance (similar to Aksyuchits' [[ruRKhDD|Christian Democratic Party]] and Astafyev's [[ruKDPPNS|Constitutional Democrats]]). The Democratic Party was opposed to the dissolution of the Soviet Union and criticised Latvia's and Estonia's policies towards their Russian-speaking minorities. After the signing of the Belovezhye treaty, the DP organized a number of demonstrations against the treaty.

In the 1993 parliamentary elections in Russia, the party received 5.52% of the Proportional Representation ballot vote (2,969,533 votes) as well as 2.1% (1,094,066 votes) of votes on individual district ballots. This translated into 14 and 7 seats, respectively, for a total of 21 seats in the 450-seat Duma.

The party's stance on Yegor Gaidar's economic reforms was confusing but developed more critical in the course of time. During the 1993 Russian constitutional crisis, the party did not have a unanimous position. The party called for balloting both for the re-election of the President as well as of the legislative bodies on the referendum in April 1993; however, some of the party's leaders took the pro-Yeltsin side. Similarly, during the October 1993 events in Moscow, Travkin initially supported the so-called zero variants (annulling both Yeltsin's decree nr 1400 and the Supreme Soviet's subsequent decisions). On 4 October, Travkin supported Yeltsin's actions in suppressing the armed rebellion. The party split, however, on the issue of support for the Chernomyrdin cabinet. Travkin who took a more conciliatory stand lost the power struggle to Govorukhin and Glazyev, who were determined opponents of the government course, and Travkin consequently left the party and joined the [[ruNDR|Our Home – Russia]] movement.

Glazyev was made the leader in 1994 but was disbanded before the following year's legislative election. The rump DRP split further between Govorukhin and Glazyev supporters. In the 1995 Russian legislative election, the Glazyev wing took part within the Congress of Russian Communities list, whilst Govorukhin formed his own list, called the Stanislav Govorukhin Bloc.

In the 1996 presidential election, the Democratic Party supported Alexander Lebed, though some of its regional leaders supported Yeltsin's campaign. In the 2000 presidential election, the party supported Vladimir Putin.

In 2001 the party was reformed by Mikhail Prusak. In 2005 Mikhail Kasyanov tried to be elected chairman of the party, but lost to Andrei Bogdanov. In June 2007, the party proposed a referendum on joining the European Union and in December it took part in the legislative election, but it did not win any seats. The DPR of that time was accused of being a virtual party used to draw away votes from the real opposition parties.

17 September 2007, with the support of the [[euEPP|European People's Party]] in the headquarters of the European Union in Brussels, hosted the XXI Congress of the Democratic Party of Russia, which adopted the decision on the accession of Russia to the European Union.

In the 2007 Russian legislative election the party won 0.13% of votes, not breaking the 7% barrier, and thus no seats in the Duma. As of 1 January 2007, according to the Federal Registration Service, the party had 82,183 members.

According to the results of the regional elections of 2012, 2013, and 2014, the party failed to win in regional and city parliaments.

In 2014 Andrei Bogdanov head created by the participation of the [[ruRPSS|Communist Party of Social Justice]], leader of the Democratic Party of Russia was elected his brother Timur Bogdanov.

In 2020, the party nominated two single-mandate candidates for the State Council of the Komi Republic, but only one, Igor Egorov, was registered. Alexey Utkin, a candidate for governor of the Kostroma Oblast, was also denied registration. Evgenia Pasternak, a sole proprietor and candidate for governor of the Jewish Autonomous Oblast, was also denied registration.

The party announced their support for incumbent president Vladimir Putin in the 2024 presidential election, after DPR candidate Irina Sviridova got her registration denied.

parties.name: Green Alternative
parties.description:
The Green Alternative was created by Kremlin political strategist Vyacheslav Smirnov. 

Ruslan Khvostov, an environmental activist, member of the Moscow Region Civic Chamber, and former coordinator of the "Ecological Expedition" project of the youth environmental movement "[[ruMestnye|Mestnye]]" (2016-2018), was elected party chairman. From December 2019 to March 2020, the Green Alternative existed as a social movement. The congress was attended by representatives of the previously liquidated [[ruAZ|Green Alliance]] party.

Renowned artist Alexei Kudelin (known as Vasya Lozhkin) became the party's informal leader. His cat drawings served as the basis for the party's logo.

According to Khvostov, the party has nothing in common with the 2009-2012 movement of the same name, the [[ruGROZA|Civil United Green Alternative]] (GROZA), which was led by Oleg Mitvol.

According to party members, the Green Alternative is not exclusively associated with the environmental movement, but rather qualifies as a "moderate left-wing environmental party of the European type." In 2021, Green Alternative applied to join the [[euEGP|European Green Party]].

In June 2020, the party proposed erecting a monument to environmental activist Greta Thunberg in the center of Moscow's Hyde Park in Sokolniki.

The party contested the 2020 regional elections, receiving 10% of the vote in the Komi Republic and 5.4% in the Chelyabinsk Oblast, and winning a seat in both federal subjects' parliaments. Because the party won seats in regional parliaments, it gained the right to participate in federal parliamentary elections without collecting signatures.

In the 2021 legislative elections, Green Alternative came twelfth, winning 0.64% of the popular vote and no seats.

On 26 April 2026, in anticipation of the 2026 State Duma election, the party merged with the [[ruREPZ|Russian Ecological Party "The Greens"]] by decision of the general congress.

parties.description:
Successor of the [[suLDPSU|Liberal Democratic Party of the Soviet Union]] in Russia. The party was led by Vladimir Zhirinovsky since its inception until his death in April 2022. Opposing both communism and state capitalism of the 1990s, the party scored a major success in the 1993 Duma elections with almost 23% of the vote, giving it 64 seats of the 450 seats in the State Duma. In the 2021 elections, the party received 7.55% of the vote, giving it 21 seats.

Despite the party's name, it has been described as "neither liberal nor democratic nor a party". The LDPR was centered around Zhirinovsky, and is often described as populist, nationalist, or ultranationalist. It has been described as adhering to statism and authoritarianism, and has also been described as fascist, though this label has been disputed. The party, as part of the "systemic opposition", is considered to be traditionally loyal to the Kremlin. Besides the aforementioned accusations, it has also been described as right-liberal. The party has been a part of the federal government since 14 May 2024, with Mikhail Degtyarev serving as Minister of Sport.

parties.name: New People
parties.description:
In January 2020, businessmen, CEO of Faberlic cosmetic company, Alexey Nechayev announced the party's creation to the media.

On 1 March 2020, the constituent congress of New People was held. 55 party regional branches were created. Official party registration was received from the Russian Ministry of Justice at the end of March.

As of 1 July 2020, New People had 55 registered regional branches, which began preparing to take part in the regional elections of September 2020 in 12 regions of the country. Also, the party declared its readiness and intent to take part in the elections to the State Duma in 2021.

On 8 August 2020, the second congress of the party was held in Moscow at which its founder Alexey Nechayev was elected chairman of the party.

On 4 July 2021, a party congress was held at which the party's list and candidates for participation in the 2021 legislative election were nominated. Party leader Alexey Nechayev headed the federal list of the party. The second number in the federal list was the former Mayor of Yakutsk Sardana Avksentyeva.

According to the election results, the party gained 5.3% of the vote, winning 13 seats in the State Duma. New People became the first party not from the "big four" ([[ruER|United Russia]], [[ruKPRF|KPRF]], [[ruLDPR|LDPR]] and [[ruSR|SRZP]]) since 2007 to overcome the 5% barrier and form its own faction. In addition to the 13 deputies elected on the party list of the party, the New People faction also included two independent deputies elected in single-mandate constituencies: Dmitry Pevtsov and Oleg Leonov.

On 15 February 2022, New People's Duma faction voted against the recognition of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions as independent states. However, the party later withdrew its statement and proclaimed its support for the 2022 war.

On 16 August 2022, the party called for Instagram to be unblocked.

On 24 December 2023, it was reported that the [[ruROST|Party of Growth]] will be merged with New People, both parties are already part of the informal political alliance [[ruSPPS|Union of Progressive Political Forces]]. At a joint congress on 19 April 2024, the New People and the Growth Party announced a legal unification, and all delegates voted for the unification. The parties will operate under the general name “New People”. Growth Party leader Boris Titov will head the federal political council. The only State Duma deputy from the Growth Party, Oksana Dmitriyeva, announced that she would take the position of chairwoman of the regional branch of New People in Saint Petersburg. At the same time, she stated that she did not intend to join the New People faction in the Duma.

During the 2024 presidential campaign, some opposition forces considered Vladislav Davankov's New People's party as a target for protest voting after the Central Election Commission refused to register Boris Nadezhdin.

parties.name: Party of Business
parties.literalName: Party of the Cause / Party of Action
parties.description:
The Party of Business was described as a spoiler for [[ruPD|Right Cause]] (also abbreviated PD), trying to draw business-affiliated votes away from it.

On 22 September 2010, a group of economists and entrepreneurs announced the imminent formation of a new party called the Party of Business. On 14 October 2010, the party's founding congress was held at the Izmailovo Hotel in Moscow, where 160 delegates from 51 regions of Russia approved the party's program and charter.

On 12 October 2010, a picket against the reduction of agricultural subsidies was held near the Russian Ministry of Agriculture building. Twenty people participated in the picket. On 3 November 2010, a picket against Russia's accession to the WTO was held at the same building. Party activists promised to hold rallies every Wednesday until Agriculture Minister Elena Skrynnik acknowledges the decision to reduce agricultural subsidies to WTO levels was a mistake. Since then, pickets on this issue have been held almost weekly. At one of them, even employees of the Ministry of Agriculture expressed support for the protesters.

On 10 November 2010, the first founding conference of the party's regional branch was held in the Republic of Bashkortostan. By 1 December, regional branches had been formed in 42 regions of Russia, which is sufficient to gain the status of an all-Russian political party.

On 27 December 2010, the party submitted documents for registration to the Ministry of Justice. In February 2011, the party was denied registration. The Ministry of Justice's decision was appealed in court.

On 4 April 2012, the registration process for the referendum on Russia's accession to the WTO was launched in the building of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Russia – the first meeting of the organizing committee and a meeting of the Moscow regional subgroup. More than 300 people attended the meeting of the regional subgroup, which was held in the building of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Moscow. The initiators were the public organization Russian People's Cathedral, the [[ruPGR|Trade Union of Citizens of Russia]], the Interregional Public Organization VECHE, and the Party of Business On 13 April, the Russian Central Election Commission deemed it impossible to hold a referendum in Russia on the country's accession to the World Trade Organization.

On 31 October 2012, delegates from Russia's regional branches held a new Founding Congress, at which they decided to establish the Party of Business along with its Charter and Program. On 14 December 2012, the party was registered by the Ministry of Justice.

On 5 March 2015, party members held their Second Congress to admit new members to the Federal Council, adopt a new version of the program, and discuss the development of the Non-Black Earth Region regions. The congress was held in Kostroma.

In 2016, members of the Party of Business won more seats in the Spassky Municipal District Duma elections in Primorsky Krai than representatives of [[ruER|United Russia]].

On 27 November 2017, the IV Congress of the Party of Business was held, where delegates supported the inclusion of new managers in the party's governing bodies.

The party’s activities were suspended by Russia’s Supreme Court in April 2024 after violations were found in the party’s charter. On 18 October 2024, Russia’s Ministry of Justice requested to dissolve the party. On 27 November 2024, the Party of Business was liquidated by the Supreme Court of the Russian Federation. After the dissolution of the party, Konstantin Babkin was accepted into the Supreme Council of the [[ruLDPR|Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]].

parties.description:
The creation of the Direct Democracy Party was publicly announced on January 10, 2020. On March 5 of that year, a founding congress was held, at which its charter was adopted, a general secretary, and the first Supreme Coordination Council were elected. The party's founder, Vyacheslav Makarov, became its general secretary.

On April 1, 2020, the party was registered by the Ministry of Justice of the Russian Federation.

In November 2020, Vyacheslav Makarov resigned as general secretary, citing a lack of long-term political plans and the need to immediately launch the party. Oleg Artamonov, head of the party's scientific and technical expertise, was elected as the new general secretary at an extraordinary congress.

In January 2021, the party's general secretary, Oleg Artamonov, announced that the party would not participate in the State Duma elections, focusing on elections to regional parliaments. In the 2021 elections to the Legislative Assembly of the Jewish Autonomous Region, the Direct Democracy Party received 5.93% of the vote, winning one seat.

In 2022 and 2023, the party barely participated in the elections, nominating only three candidates for local government, two of whom were denied registration.

In 2024, a by-election for a State Duma deputy in Khakassia's single-mandate constituency No. 35 was held. Anton Palyulin became the party's candidate. Palyulin received 1.79% of the vote (fifth place out of six candidates).

The Direct Democracy Party advocates the establishment of direct democracy through digitalization, expanding the capabilities of the application "Gosuslugi" to control the activities of deputies and elected officials, providing residents of municipalities with the opportunity to directly distribute part of the local budget. At the same time, the party refuses to approve any official ideology, since the policy of elected deputies should be determined directly on the ground by voters.

parties.name: Party of Progress
parties.description:
The Party of Social Networks (PSS) was founded on 9 April 2012, and officially registered on May 29, 2012. It was created with the participation of Andrei Bogdanov, leader of the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] and the Center for Political Technologies. The party did not publicly identify itself, had no website or official social media group, and nothing is known about its composition or official leadership, including its chairman, Dmitry Chirov. Similar parties created by Andrei Bogdanov are called party businesses, nominating candidates on a commercial basis and selling ready-made parties on a turnkey basis. The party's membership in 2012 was 500 (the minimum required number of members for political party registration following the May amendments to Federal Law No. 95-FZ).

The Party of Social Networks relied on a social-liberal ideology, advocating for an end to state funding of religious organizations, a reduction in military spending with a mass transition to a contract basis, the abolition of the Federation Council and a transition to a unicameral system of legislative power. In the regional elections, the PSS used the email symbol @ as its logo.

On 12 April 2013, at the Third Congress, the Party of Social Networks was reorganized into the Civic Position party, and Vladimir Albertovich Vekselman was elected Chairman of the Federal Council.

The Civic Position logo was almost identical to the [[ruGP|Civic Platform]] logo. On 22 May 2013, it was announced that Alexei Chesnakov, former Deputy Secretary of the General Council of the [[ruER|United Russia]] party and political scientist, intended to lead the Civil Position party. However, he never took over the party.

In 2012–2013, "Civic Position" participated in local elections in several regions of Russia; In particular, in the parliaments of Chechnya, Yakutia, and the Vladimir region. During the Vladimir elections, the party submitted a document to the local electoral commission containing information on the candidates' income and assets, according to which none of the 17 candidates owned any property or received any income for 2012. The electoral commission deemed this information inaccurate. The party's best result was 0.26%, which it received in the fall of 2012 in the elections to the Legislative Assembly of Krasnodar Krai. 

Following Vekselman, Andrei Poda, owner of the Madeleine Travel Salon, became chairman of the Civil Position political council in 2016. In 2015, Poda founded the public organization Investment Russia in Mordovia, also associated with Andrei Bogdanov.

In 2015, Andrei Bogdanov, speaking to Vedomosti, mentioned Civil Position among "his" parties. At the time, he offered to buy the party for at least $250,000.

On 22 February 2018, Vitaly Serukanov, former deputy head of Alexei Navalny's Moscow presidential campaign headquarters, announced on Facebook that he had submitted documents to the Ministry of Justice to register the Party of Progress based on the "Civil Position" party. This is also the name of the [[ruRB|unregistered party of Navalny and his supporters]], but Serukanov's organization has no connection to it. Navalny claimed that political strategist Andrei Bogdanov was trying to steal the party from him.

Serukanov stated that he did not know whether Bogdanov had any connection to Civil Position and that he was negotiating with "completely different people." He declined to name these people until the transformation process was complete. Serukanov noted that he had been a member of the Party of Progress since its founding, and now he and a group of like-minded individuals had "united to develop a new socio-political force without leaders or armchair theorists."

On 19 March 2018, the Unified State Register of Legal Entities (USRLE) recorded changes to the founding documents of the Civil Position party, according to which it was renamed the Party of Progress. Due to the registration of the Party of Progress, supporters of Alexei Navalny were forced to choose a new name for their party. Navalny's party was renamed [[ruRB|Russia of the Future]].

parties.description:
The party was established at its founding congress on 5 May 2012. Delegates from 53 regions attended the congress. The process of official registration of the party in the Unified State Register of Legal Entities by the Ministry of Justice was completed on 19 June 2012. Viktor Sviridov became the party's first leader.

PSZ candidate Viktor Perov ran for governor of Saint Petersburg in 2019. Previously, Viktor Perov was a member of the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] and the [[ruKPKR|Communists of Russia]]. He was also a deputy of the Slantsy Municipal Council. If he wins the gubernatorial election, Perov promises to build "developed socialism" in Saint Petersburg.

The Krasnodar branch of the party held a rally in July 2019 against the increase in public transport fares.

The party held two seats in the Kostroma Regional Duma (2020-2025).

In June 2022, a picket “No to nuclear war!” was held in Kostroma, approved by the authorities and initiated by Vladimir Mikhailov.

By the decision of the Supreme Court of Russia of 18 December 2025, which entered into force on 12 March 2026, the activities of the Political Party of Social Protection, its regional branches and other structural divisions were suspended for a period of two months. On 3 June 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the Ministry of Justice's request to liquidate the Party of Social Protection. According to the Ministry of Justice, the organization failed to correct violations identified during the previous year's inspection. In particular the party provided false information about its members: about two dozen people listed on the register turned out to be [[ruER|United Russia]] members.

parties.description:
Established in April 2005 by Gennady Semigin, who was expelled from the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of the Russian Federation]] after he failed in a power struggle with Gennady Zyuganov. Legally, Patriots of Russia is a successor party of the [[ruRPT|Russian Party of Labour]].

In 2006 Gennadiy Semigin and his new Patriots of Russia party joined the [[ruRodina2005|Rodina]] faction in the Duma. Following Rodina's merger with the [[ruRPZh|Russian Party of Life]] and the [[ruRPP|Russian Party of Pensioners]] under the leadership of Sergey Mironov in October 2006 to form the [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] party, Patriots of Russia declared its intention to run as a separate party in the 2007 State Duma election. In the 2007 election, members of the unregistered [[ruVR2007|Great Russia]] party participated on the Patriots of Russia list.

In 2008, the VIII Congress approved the self-dissolution of the [[ruPME|Party of Peace and Unity]] (PME) and its entry into the Patriots of Russia party. However, in 2012, following legislative amendments to simplify the registration of political parties, the PME organizing committee decided to reinstate itself and leave the Patriots of Russia party.

The [[ruPVR|Party of Russia's Rebirth]] (PVR) merged into the Patriots of Russia on 9 September 2008. PVR was re-established on 26 October 2012.

In December 2017, the Patriots of Russia announced that they would not run in the 2018 Russian presidential election and that the party would support current president Vladimir Putin for the elections.

Since 2011, the party has been an ally of the [[ruONF|All-Russia People's Front]] (ONF), created at the initiative of Vladimir Putin.

Until 2021, PR maintained close ties with the [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] party, which it subsequently joined. In February 2021, PR (together with [[ruZP|For Truth]]) merged into the [[ruSR|A Just Russia – Patriots – For Truth]] party.

As a political movement, it continues to exist to this day.

parties.name: Rodina
parties.description:
On 21 September 2011, the [[ruKRO|Congress of Russian Communities]], a public association, held a congress, at which the organization was reorganized into Rodina-Congress of Russian Communities. An organizing committee was created to restore the Rodina political party, which in 2006 co-founded [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] (SR). (In 2006, Rodina was led by Alexander Babakov, who attempted to give it a social democratic bent.) At the congress, Dmitry Rogozin accused SR leader Sergei Mironov of "hostile takeover" of the Rodina party.

In April 2012, the "Rodina-Congress of Russian Communities" organizing committee filed a notice with the Ministry of Justice to reinstate the political party.

On 29 September 2012, the founding congress of the "All-Russian Political Party «Rodina»" and the Special Purpose Volunteer Movement (DON) was held in Moscow. Delegates declared the full restoration of Rodina's organizational and political independence. Alexei Zhuravlev, a State Duma deputy from [[ruER|United Russia]], member of the Presidential Council for Interethnic Relations and chairman of the public organization [[ruKRO|Congress of Russian Communities]], was elected chairman of the party and the DON volunteer movement.

The party opposed the 2011–2013 Russian protests and members of the party's paramilitary have participated in attacks on migrants in Moscow.

The party's 2016 economic program was based on works by economist Sergei Glazyev. Its elements include the acquisition of "economic sovereignty," necessary under the current sanctions regime "and state capitalism with elements of a planned economy." In addition, sections were being prepared on the army and the defense industry, as well as the development of the Arctic region. In 2016 State Duma election Alexei Zhuravlev himself ran as a [[ru|ONF|ONF]]-supported candidate in the 89th Anninsky single-mandate constituency of the Voronezh Region, where he won. He was re-elected in 2021.

In July 2017, the Rodina party announced that it would not nominate a candidate in the 2018 Russian presidential elections, but would support the incumbent President Vladimir Putin. At the congress, the [[ruRSP|Russian Socialist Party]] merged into Rodina.

In December 2017, the former chairman of the [[ruRPPSS|Party of Pensioners]], Igor Zotov, was elected secretary of the political council of the Rodina party.

In December 2023, Rodina announced that the party will support current President Vladimir Putin for the 2024 presidential election.

parties.nativeName:
Российский общенародный союз
Rossiyskiy obshchenarodnyy soyuz
parties.description:
A Russian political party formed in October 1991. Until 2011, it operated as a political movement.

The organization was founded by Russian nationalist-oriented members of the Russian Platform of the [[suCPSU|CPSU]], and was launched on 26 October 1991 by Russian Supreme Soviet deputies of the faction Rossiya. According to Nikolai Pavlov, one of the ROS leaders, the party was established as a "patriotic and democratic" force with the aim of uniting parties of socialist orientation. Pavlov also stated that they had similar positions with more centrist organizations like the [[ruKDPPNS|Kadet Party]] of Mikhail Astafyev, Viktor Aksiuchits' [[ruRKhDD|Christian Democratic Party of Russia]], and the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]]; one of the ROS member organizations in 1992 was the [[ruRPK|Russian Party of Communists]], which was led by Anatoly Kryuchkov. The ROS was part of the United Opposition and later [[ruFNS|National Salvation Front]], belonging to the FNS right-wing faction. Besides socialist tendencies, the ROS had connections with traditional Russian nationalists and monarchists, and promoted pan-Slavist policies, including support for Serbia's expansion.

The party published newspaper Vremya (Time). The ROS took part in the 1995 Russian legislative election within the bloc [[ruVlNa|Power to the People!]], which was led by Baburin and Nikolai Ryzhkov. It won 1.6% of votes, failing to pass the 5% barrier; the ROS got nine seats, all from majoritarian districts. The party co-operated with other formations of nationalist-communist orientation, such as the [[ruKPRF|Communist Party of Russian Federation]], whose candidate Gennady Zyuganov (supported by the ROS) was defeated in the 1996 Russian presidential election by incumbent Boris Yeltsin. In 2001, the ROS joined with three other nationalist parties to form the [[ruNarS|Narodnaya Volya/People's Union]]. In 2008, the ROS was reorganized when People's Union dissolved itself.

On 22 December 2017, the ROS nominated Sergey Baburin as its candidate for the 2018 Russian presidential election. On 24 December, Baburin filed registration documents with the Central Election Commission (CEC). The CEC rejected Baburin's bid on 25 December because it identified violations in the information provided regarding 18 of his party's 48 representatives.[8] Baburin resubmitted the documents, and they were approved by the CEC.

Baburin was nominated by his party again in December 2023 during the party's congress. He submitted documents to participate in the election on 26 December, which were registered on 29 December. Baburin collected the required number of signatures, but decided to withdraw on the day before the deadline to submit signatures 30 January 2024 and endorsed Putin for the 2024 election.

In June 2025, the Russian Ministry of Justice filed a lawsuit in the Supreme Court to liquidate ROS, citing the party's failure to participate in elections over the past seven years. On 21 July 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the claim, liquidating the party. The party's leader, Sergey Baburin, expressed his disagreement with its dissolution, calling it a "political action."

parties.description:
Communist Party of Social Justice (KPSS, same abbreviation as [[suCPSU|CPSU]]) was founded on 9 April 2012 with the participation of Andrei Bogdanov, leader of the [[ruDPR|Democratic Party of Russia]] and the Center for Political Technologies. This was announced on 18 July 2012, at a joint press conference of the "Coordinating Council - Inter-Party Conference" - an association that was also created on the initiative of Andrei Bogdanov.

In the 2013 regional elections in Volgograd, it received 5.04% (9,055 votes), overcoming the 5% threshold and winning one seat in the Volgograd City Duma.

In 2014, Andrei Bogdanov himself became the party's leader, replacing Yuri Morozov. Andrei Brezhnev, the grandson of Leonid Brezhnev, General Secretary of the [[suCPSU|CPSU]] Central Committee, was elected First Secretary of the party's KPSS Central Committee. Brezhnev headed the party lists in the elections, which resulted in the party receiving 2.21% (5,085 votes) in the State Assembly of the Republic of Mari El. However, on 18 December 2015, Oleg Sidorov was removed from office.

KPSS did not participate in the 2016 State Duma elections. The Central Electoral Commission did not include the party in the list of parties exempt from collecting voter signatures for the State Duma elections. The party did not independently collect signatures.

On 12 January 2018, the secretary of the party's Central Committee and Volgograd City Duma deputy Oleg Bulaev submitted documents to the Russian Central Electoral Commission for the 2018 Russian presidential election, but withdrew his candidacy before registration.

On 28 March 2021, at the KPSS congress, former State Duma deputy of the 5th convocation (from the [[ruER|United Russia]] faction) and political strategist Konstantin Rykov was elected as the new chairman of the party's Central Committee. Iit was decided to change the party's name to the "Russian Party of Freedom and Justice" (RPSS).

On 29 March 2021, news sources reported that public figure and journalist Maxim Shevchenko may run for the State Duma from the RPSS. Shevchenko himself confirmed that this issue was being considered. On March 31, the first party conference was held, during which an agreement was reached on Shevchenko's nomination for the 208th (Central) electoral district of Moscow. The politician will also head the party's federal list and become its leader.

On 15 April 2021, Maxim Shevchenko's YouTube channel announced the first candidates from the RPSS party list for the upcoming State Duma elections. They were entrepreneur and economist Dmitry Potapenko and expert on the North Caucasus and Islam, Ruslan Kurbanov.

On 27 April 2021, Moscow City Duma deputy Elena Shuvalova, previously expelled from the [[ruKPRF|KPRF]] for voting against the Moscow budget and organizing a roundtable with Navalny supporters, was presented as the party's candidate. She topped the party's Moscow list. On 8 May, Maxim Kukushkin, a deputy of the Khabarovsk Krai Legislative Duma who had previously been expelled from the [[ruKPRF|KPRF]] for participating in a pro-Navalny rally on 23 January 2021, was presented as the party's candidate.

Like its predecessor KPSS, RPSS party was described as a spoiler for the Communist Party of the Russian Federation in the 2021 State Duma elections, in which it received only 0.77 votes.

On 9 September 2022, Maxim Shevchenko announced on his official Telegram channel that he no longer considers himself the leader of the RPSS and is no longer involved in the party's activities.

In 2022, the party's official website (https://rpss.ru/) was shut down for non-payment.

In December 2023, Andrei Bogdanov ran for the RPSS in the 2024 presidential election, but withdrew from the race in January 2024.
