parties.description:
Direct successor to the [[ruRPP|Russian Party of Pensioners]] (RPP), which was dissolved in 2006 as a result of a merger with [[ruRodina2006|Rodina]] and the [[ruRPZh|Russian Party of Life]] to form [[ruSR|A Just Russia]].

Following the RPP's dissolution, on 4 September 2007, the public organization "Russian Pensioners" was created on its basis, chaired by former party leader Igor Zotov.

In February 2012, the Pensioners' Party announced its withdrawal from [[ruSR|A Just Russia]] and its support for Vladimir Putin, as well as the holding of a party congress.

On 7 April 2012, a congress of the public organization "Russian Pensioners for Justice" was held, at which a decision was made to establish a political party with a new name, "Russian Party of Pensioners for Justice," while retaining its previous symbols. Igor Zotov, a deputy of the 6th State Duma, who had led the Pensioners' Party since December 2005, was elected party chairman.

On 13 June 2012, the Pensioners' Party was officially registered by the Ministry of Justice.

On 27 November 2015, Igor Zotov resigned as party chairman. On 26 December 2015, at the party congress, Yevgeny Artyukh, a deputy of the Legislative Assembly of the Sverdlovsk Oblast and Vladimir Putin's confidant in the 2012 presidential election, was elected RPPS chairman.

In July 2016, the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation removed 42 candidates from the party's federal list, citing errors and missing information in the submitted documents. Artyukh later stated that pressure was exerted on the party to remove candidates "not cleared" with the Presidential Administration. On 29 July Yevgeny Artyukh was removed from his leadership position and later withdrew from the Sverdlovsk Oblast elections. Vladimir Burakov became chairman. 

On 11 March 2017, the party changed its name to the "Russian Party of Pensioners for Social Justice," changed its emblem, and abolished the position of chairman.

In 2018 the party announced that they would support incumbent president Vladimir Putin in the 2018 presidential election. Putin ultimately won with approximately 77% of the vote.

In the 2021 State Duma elections, the party received 2.45% of the vote, becoming the largest among those that failed to pass the 5% threshold.

In 2023 the party again announced that they support incumbent president Vladimir Putin in the 2024 presidential election.

Vladimir Burakov died at the age of 70 on December 23, 2024, as a result of a long illness. In May 2025, Eric Prazdnikov was elected as the new RPPSS chairman.

parties.name: Workers' Power
parties.description:
The organization was formed in September 2024. Its founders had previously been members of the [[ruOKI|Organization of Communists-Internationalists]] (OKI), a section of the international organization called the [[intRCI|Revolutionary Communist International]], but left the OCI due to a split. The OKI was created in May 2023 through the merger of the [[ruNK|New Reds]] and [[ruMT|Marxist Tendency]].

At Workers' Power meetings, they held film screenings and exhibitions, discussed industry's contribution to climate change, discussed workers' rights, supported political prisoners with leftist views (such as Boris Kagarlitsky), addressed the problems of teachers, and economic inequality. The organization's manifesto, published in March 2025, offered a left-wing analysis of the current situation in capitalist countries, including Russia, and called for the unification of communist forces and the working masses to combat socioeconomic problems and, ultimately, the creation of a communist party to mobilize the masses to destroy capitalism.

In April 2025, Russian law enforcement agencies turned their attention to Workers' Power after an anonymous group of St. Petersburg State University students, the Office for Work with the Administration (URA), claimed responsibility for an action in which unknown individuals hung a doll depicting the goddess Minerva on a monument to Count Uvarov, with the note "Science is dead." The state-run Russian media outlet RIA Novosti, citing a source in the security forces, reported the "discovery" of a cell at St. Petersburg State University consisting of "unemployed students from wealthy families" that was part of an "international network with a command center in the UK." Workers' Power and URA denied any connection between the organizations.

A few weeks after the action, two students were arrested for organizing it and sentenced to a fine of 20,000 rubles and three days in jail, respectively. The URA denied the students' affiliation with their organization, and the students themselves claimed to be unaware of the existence of either the URA or Workers' Power. On 13 May 2025, the Primorsky District Court fined the lead singer of the musical group Silver Machine 20,000 rubles for the satirical song "Za Nashikh." The song's lyrics contained ironic calls to go to war "for the masters, their comfort" and "for Gazprom and Tinkoff" at the call of the "genetic code." The court found the song's content aimed at inciting "hatred or hostility" and "humiliating human dignity based on gender, race, nationality, language, origin, religious affiliation, or social group."

On 15 May 2025, searches were conducted at students' homes at St. Petersburg universities; The published photographs show dozens of printed copies of the Workers' Power manifesto. Six people were detained and one of them was reportedly beaten. A criminal case was opened against Garry Azaryan, a student at St. Petersburg State University from Kazakhstan, for "calls to terrorism." According to investigators, from January to February 2025, Azaryan publicly expressed slogans "justifying terrorist activity, allegedly verbally called for mass murder, and planned to use students to carry out direct action." The case was opened based on an audio recording from an informal meeting, where Azaryan discussed revolution, class hatred, and the "power of the street." Azaryan denied the charges: "Our goal is not to incite hatred; we are not extremists. Our goal is to explain to people that capitalism is to blame." In September 2025, it was reported that Azaryan had been sent for a forensic psychiatric examination at the request of the investigation.

On 22 May 2025, Workers' Power announced its dissolution due to "mounting police pressure" and the risk of mass arrests and persecution. On 11 February 2026, Azaryan was sentenced to two years in prison.

parties.description:
A social liberal political party in Russia, founded as a Yavlinsky–Boldyrev–Lukin (YaBL) bloc in October 1993. Yabloko positions itself as "Russia's only democratic party". A number of political scientists and researchers characterize Yabloko as the only legally registered party in the country that stands in actual opposition to the current government. Party representatives and independent observers state that the Yabloko's members face systemic government pressure and repression.

The party consequently participated in the elections of deputies of the State Duma of all eight convocations. Until 2003, Yabloko was represented by a faction in the State Duma and later until 2007 by individual deputies. In March 2002, the party became a full member of the Liberal International, having previously held observer status since November 1998. The founder of the party Grigory Yavlinsky is an honorary vice-president of the Liberal International and winner of its Prize for Freedom. Yabloko was a member of the [[euALDE|Alliance of Liberals and Democrats for Europe]] from 2006 to 2025. As of 2021, the party was represented by factions in 4 regional parliaments of the Russian Federation. In addition, members of the party were deputies of 13 administrative centers of the subjects of the Russian Federation, 183 representatives of the party were municipal deputies in Moscow and 84 in Saint Petersburg.

Yabloko is the sole officially registered party to openly oppose the Russo-Ukrainian war, openly calling "for peace and freedom". The party plans to partake in the 2026 Russian legislative election under their anti-war slogan.

parties.description:
A political party in São Tomé and Príncipe. It was founded on 4 November 1990 by [[stMLSTPPSD|Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe]] (MLSTP) dissidents, independents, and young professionals. Leonel Mário d'Alva is the party leader.

The one-party period of São Tomé and Príncipe lasted from the country's independence in 1975 to 1991, when the dominant party, Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party, lost in the first multiparty elections to the PCD-GR. The party won the 1991 parliamentary election and was the ruling party from 1991 to 1994. Since 1994 its power has declined, and it has maintained coalitions with other parties, first the MLSTP and then the Forces for Change Coalition of President Fradique de Menezes. It was led for several years by Alda Bandeira.

At the legislative elections, March 3, 2002, the party won together with the Force for Change Democratic Movement-Liberal Party (MDFM-PL) 39.4% of the popular vote and 23 out of 55 seats. The same alliance won at the legislative election, held on 26 March 2006, 36.79% and 23 out of 55 seats. The party supported incumbent Fradique de Menezes in the 30 July 2006 presidential election. He was re-elected with 60.58% of the vote.

In the 2011 São Toméan presidential election, Delfim Neves represented both the PCD and the Force for Change Democratic Movement – Liberal Party (MDFM-PL), the part of the previous president, Fradique de Menezes. He won 13.9% of the vote.

In 2022 election, its candidates joined the [[stBasta|Basta Movement]].

description.text:
A political party in São Tomé and Príncipe. It was founded on 4 November 1990 by [[stMLSTPPSD|Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe]] (MLSTP) dissidents, independents, and young professionals. Leonel Mário d'Alva is the party leader.

The one-party period of São Tomé and Príncipe lasted from the country's independence in 1975 to 1991, when the dominant party, Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party, lost in the first multiparty elections to the PCD-GR. The party won the 1991 parliamentary election and was the ruling party from 1991 to 1994. Since 1994 its power has declined, and it has maintained coalitions with other parties, first the MLSTP and then the Forces for Change Coalition of President Fradique de Menezes. It was led for several years by Alda Bandeira.

At the legislative elections, March 3, 2002, the party won together with the Force for Change Democratic Movement-Liberal Party (MDFM-PL) 39.4% of the popular vote and 23 out of 55 seats. The same alliance won at the legislative election, held on 26 March 2006, 36.79% and 23 out of 55 seats. The party supported incumbent Fradique de Menezes in the 30 July 2006 presidential election. He was re-elected with 60.58% of the vote.

In the 2011 São Toméan presidential election, Delfim Neves represented both the PCD and the Force for Change Democratic Movement – Liberal Party (MDFM-PL), the part of the previous president, Fradique de Menezes. He won 13.9% of the vote.

In 2022 election, its candidates joined the [[stBasta|Basta Movement]].

parties.description:
The Committee for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, was founded in 1960 as a nationalist group opposed to Portuguese colonial rule. In 1961 it joined the CONCP with other communist and socialist groups fighting against the Portuguese Empire in Africa. The CLSTP was set up by exiles who eventually established their base in nearby Gabon. Manuel Pinto da Costa, who would eventually become President of an independent São Tomé and Príncipe, was the leader of the party. In 1972, the CLSTP became the MLSTP.

After the April 1974 Carnation Revolution in Portugal, the new government agreed to hand over power to the MLSTP. Later that year, the MLSTP was recognized as the sole legitimate representative of the Santomean people.

Following a brief period of transitional government, elections were held for a constituent assembly and the MLSTP won all 16 of its seats.

Independence was achieved on 12 July 1975, with Manuel Pinto da Costa as president and Miguel Trovoada as prime minister. The constitution promulgated on 12 December 1975, effectively vested absolute power in the President and the MLSTP became the nation's sole legal political party.

During the late 1970s and 1980s, the party's socialist orientation and in turn the nation's orientation led to strong ties with Cuba, East Germany and the Soviet Union.

In late 1989, a progressive faction within the party embarked on a transition to full multi-party system, after a debate at the national party conference.

A democratic constitution introduced by the MLSTP Central Committee was approved overwhelmingly in an August 1990 referendum.

At the MLSTP Party Congress in October 1990, Carlos Graça was appointed as the new Secretary-General, in succession to Manuel Pinto da Costa. In addition, the party's name was amended to the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe – Social Democratic Party (MLSTP/PSD).

In an extraordinary Congress of the MLSTP/PSD held in May 1998, Manuel Pinto da Costa was elected unopposed as President of the party, a post that he held until 2005.

At the party's Fourth Congress, Guilherme Posser da Costa, a former prime minister, was elected as president of the MLSTP/PSD on 27 February 2005, succeeding Pinto da Costa. There were 708 votes in favor of Posser da Costa, who was the only candidate, and three votes against him. As of June 2008, the President of the MLSTP/PSD is Joaquim Rafael Branco.

In June 2008, after Prime Minister Patrice Trovoada of the [[stADI|Independent Democratic Action]] (ADI) party was defeated in a vote of no confidence, President Fradique de Menezes asked the MLSTP/PSD to form a government, and it chose Branco to become the next prime minister. The ADI denounced Menezes' designation of the MLSTP/PSD to form a government as unconstitutional, arguing that it was too late in the parliamentary term to do so, and it took the matter to the Supreme Tribunal of Justice.

The current president of the MLSTP/PSD, Américo Barros, was elected on 7 September 2024.

Today the MLSTP/PSD has friendly relations with political parties in other Lusophone countries, including the [[ptPS|Socialist Party]] (PS) in Portugal and the [[aoMPLA|People's Movement for the Liberation of Angola]] (MPLA).

A political party on São Tomé and Príncipe founded in 2018 by António and Domingos Monteiro, who represented the [[stMLSTPPSD|Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe]] (MLSTP/PSD) in the National Assembly until May 2018. Its main base is the southernmost municipality on São Tomé, Caué. 

Until 2020 it was known as simply the Movement of Independent Citizens of São Tomé (MCISTP).

At the 2018 parliamentary elections it got 1,659 votes and won two seats in the Caué constituency. The party only received 608 votes outside of Caué.

In 2022, allied with the new [[stPUN|National Unity Party]] (PUN), the MCI/PS confirmed its presence by becoming the third largest force in the National Assembly. It campaigned among disadvantaged populations, Serviça immigrants, Angolans, and the peasant class descended from the roças (plantations).[6] It won four seats: three in Caué (with a 42% majority) and one in Lembá, while the PUN won one in Príncipe, allowing the coalition to form a parliamentary group. In the municipal elections held simultaneously, the MCI-PUN coalition won all nine seats in the Caué district, as well as one in Cantagalo.

parties.nativeName:
Либерально-демократическая партия Советского Союза
Liberal'no-demokraticheskaya partiya Sovetskogo Soyuza
parties.description:
In the summer of 1989, Vladimir Bogachyov left Lev Ubozhko's [[ruKPR|Democratic Party]], which in turn had split from the [[ruDS|Democratic Union]] in 1988 due to disagreement with its policies. Both Ubozhko and Bogachyov represented right-wing liberalism and conservatism. Toward the fall of 1989, Bogachev convened an initiative group to create a "liberal democratic party."

In late autumn, Vladimir Zhirinovsky, who had previously attempted to organize a "social democratic party of Russia" and even managed to develop a program for it, joined Bogachyov. This program was ultimately adopted as the basis, and the word "social" was replaced throughout with "liberal." According to the recollections of high-ranking KGB and [[suCPSU|CPSU]] Central Committee officials, with Zhirinovsky's arrival, the project became completely under the control of government officials and was formed at their instigation.

The formal first (founding) congress took place on 13 March 1990, at the Rusakov Palace of Culture, where the founding group received its official name, the "Liberal Democratic Party of the Soviet Union." According to recollections, this name was coined by representatives of the KGB's 5th Department shortly before the formal congress. Delegate cards, along with LDPSU membership cards, were distributed at the congress to anyone who wanted one. By the time of the first congress, the party had united 3,000 members across 31 regions of the Soviet Union. The party quickly received registration and the right to establish its own publication, the newspaper "Rech."

On 8 June 1990, Zhirinovsky and Vladimir Voronin (the future President of Moldova, [[mdPCRM|PCRM]]) founded the "Centrist Bloc of Political Parties and Movements." During autumn 1990, the bloc held a series of consultations with Nikolai Ryzhkov on the possible formation of a so-called "government of national unity" with the CPSU.

On 6 October 1990, at Bogachyov's initiative, the Second (Emergency) LDPSU Congress was held in Moscow. Zhirinovsky was expelled from the party for collaborating with the KGB, and the party was renamed the "Liberal Democratic Party." In response, an all-Union LDPSU conference with congressional powers was convened on 20 October, chaired by Zhirinovsky. Zhirinovsky amended the party charter and expelled Bogachyov and his supporters.

Between late 1990 and early 1991, the party advocated for a state of emergency in the country and a temporary ban on all political parties. On 27 February 1991, the LDPSU participated in the "For a Great, United Russia!" conference organized by the [[ruKPRSFSR|Communist Party of the RSFSR]].

On 12 April 1991, the party was formally registered by the USSR Ministry of Justice. That same year, Zhirinovsky nominated the party for the first direct presidential election in the RSFSR, finishing third with 7.81% of the vote.

During the August 1991 coup, Zhirinovsky and the LDPSU officially supported the putschists (GKChP) and welcomed their actions. After the coup's failure, the party's activities were suspended in Moscow, and the Ministry of Justice issued a warning to the party. The investigative group for the GKChP subsequently prepared charges against Zhirinovsky and the party for violating six articles of the Criminal Code, but these were never brought.

Several months after the collapse of the Soviet Union, the Third Congress of the Liberal Democratic Party was held in Moscow on 18-19 April 1992, attended by 627 delegates from 43 regions. The LDP was reorganized into the [[ruLDPR|Liberal Democratic Party of Russia]]. Zhirinovsky was again elected party chairman.

In subsequent years, in addition to the LDPR, several similar liberal democratic parties were created in the post-Soviet space:
- [[byLDPB|Liberal Democratic Party of Belarus]], a splinter of Zhirinovsky's party, reorganized in 1994;
- [[uaLDPU|Liberal Democratic Party of Ukraine]], independent of the LDPR, a group that had contacts with Bogachev's group in 1990, condemned the pro-Zhirinovsky coup of 1990, and retained a liberal and pro-Western orientation;
- [[pmrLDPP|Liberal Democratic Party of Transnistria]], previously the Transnistrian branch of the LDPR, reorganized into a separate party in 2006.
